title: When doubt comes
hookLine: companions told the Prophet ﷺ of troubling thoughts, and he called their distress at them clear faith (Muslim)
tomorrow: can someone with strong faith still cry at a hospital?

lines: TOO TERRIBLE TO SAY OUT LOUD.
cards: Half past one at night, a search bar. Is it bad to doubt God. Typed, deleted, typed again.
Some thoughts feel too heavy to say to a person, so they go to a phone instead. In Medina, a group of the companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ brought him that same kind of secret.
They came carefully, the way you carry bad news. Something comes into our minds, they told him, that each of us would find too terrible to say out loud. Then they waited for what he'd say.

teach.b: He asked them one question: do you really find that? Yes, they said.
And he answered, in the report Imam Muslim collected: that is clear faith. Not the thought itself. Their distress at it.

A thought that doesn't trouble you is just a thought. The ache is the sign that something in you cares. Another report, in Abu Dawud, has a man saying he would rather be burned to charcoal than speak what was in his head.

teach.h: A PLAN SHRUNK TO A WHISPER.
teach.b: The Prophet said Allahu akbar, and praised God that the enemy's plan had shrunk to a whisper, a waswasa. The collections give a next step, too.

A whispering voice asks who made this, who made that, until it asks who made your Lord, and the Prophet said: when it gets there, seek refuge in Allah, and stop. That's for the whisper that circles and circles.
A question you truly want answered is a different thing; people bring those to someone who knows, and to God. Either way, the story starts with what the companions did before he said a word.
They named it, to the one person who could help them carry it.

how: Muslims troubled by passing doubts often say a'udhu billah, seeking refuge in God, and turn away from the whisper; questions they want answered they bring to a teacher or scholar they trust, and to God in du'a.

o: the moment a question about God unsettles you
a test from God that only the weak fail
the day you finally decide God isn't real

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: seek refuge in Allah, and stop
named it instead of hiding it

s: having a doubt about God means your faith is gone
the Prophet called the companions' distress at such thoughts clear faith.
the companions said the thoughts were too terrible to speak
he asked, do you really find that? then said: that is clear faith.
the hadith praises the doubting thought itself
it's the distress at the thought, not the thought, that he called faith.

games.q: at bedtime your little brother whispers that he sometimes wonders if God is real, and he's scared he's a bad Muslim. what fits the hadith?
o: good Muslims never think that, so he should just stop.
being bothered by the thought is itself a sign of faith.
everybody has doubts; it means nothing, so forget it.
games.why: the companions felt the same fear, and the Prophet called their distress clear faith. it's also a sentence a parent can say at bedtime.

practice: Find the doubt you've been carrying, the one you'd type and delete. Say it once, quietly, in plain words.
If you pray, say it to Allah, the way the companions brought theirs into the open; if not, say it to the room, and notice how it sounds out loud. Then sit with whatever is left.

wordCard.voice: When doubt comes: the thought you'd hate to say. The companions' distress at it, the Prophet said, was clear faith.

orig.note: Arabic: clear faith, the Prophet's words for the companions' distress at their thoughts (Muslim).

carryVoice: Keep this one: troubled by it means faith, a sign of what you care about. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 132 (companions troubled by thoughts too terrible to speak: 'that is clear faith')
Sunan Abi Dawud 5112 (rather be burned to charcoal; 'reduced his plot to a whisper')
Sahih Muslim 134; Sahih al-Bukhari 3276 (who created your Lord? seek refuge in Allah and stop)
